reading.title: Reading fiber descriptions
reading.text: At a textile workshop, Rami separates fiber names from weave names. Cotton comes from cotton plants, silk from silk-producing larvae, wool from sheep, and linen from flax. Cashmere concerns qualifying goat hair; it is not a synonym for any soft cloth. Hemp and jute are plant fibers. A bamboo description needs clarification because many such textiles are rayon made from bamboo-derived cellulose. Mohair comes from Angora goats, whereas alpaca fiber comes from alpacas. Polyester, nylon, acrylic and spandex are synthetic fiber names. Rayon is manufactured from processed cellulose. Rami checks the declared composition before interpreting a sample. Color and softness cannot establish the fiber, and blends may contain several fibers. The workshop compares terminology rather than identifies an unknown sample from a photograph.

reading.title: Distinguishing brands and fabric structures
reading.text: Rami finds that fabric descriptions use several kinds of name. Lycra is a trademark for elastane fiber; microfiber describes very fine fibers rather than one specific polymer. Gore-Tex and Kevlar are trademarks associated with different material technologies. Neoprene is synthetic rubber. Velvet has a pile surface, whereas satin describes a weave producing a smooth face and may use different fibers. Chiffon is lightweight and sheer. Organza is a crisp sheer fabric, and taffeta is crisp with a smoother closed surface. Brocade uses patterned weaving, while Jacquard describes a patterning system or the resulting fabric. Crepe has a textured or crinkled appearance. Tulle is netting, and lace has an open decorative structure. Rami asks about composition and construction separately; a branded name alone does not prove a performance claim.

reading.title: Comparing construction, properties and care
reading.text: Rami examines construction before discussing care. A weave interlaces yarns; a knit forms interconnected loops. Warp runs along the weaving direction, and weft crosses it. Thread count measures yarn density under a stated method, not overall quality by itself. Weight concerns mass per area. Drape describes how fabric hangs, stretch how it extends, and breathability how it permits air or moisture vapor to pass. Durability concerns resistance to wear or damage. Hand wash and machine wash describe different cleaning methods; dry clean uses cleaning solvents in an appropriate professional process. Iron and steam concern finishing or refreshing cloth. Rami reads the actual care instructions rather than assumes one method suits every fiber, garment finish or blend. The workshop provides vocabulary, not a care procedure for an unknown item.

reading.title: Interpreting laundry terms
reading.text: Rami reads five terms on a fictional care worksheet. Bleach can mean treating cloth with a bleaching agent, but suitability depends on the actual instructions. Tumble dry means using a rotating dryer; line dry means hanging an item to dry. Stain removal concerns dealing with an unwanted mark, rather than one universal chemical or method. Fabric softener is a laundry product intended to change the fabric's feel. Rami does not combine these actions into a recipe. He asks which instructions belong to the specific garment and checks the product information. A bottle's appearance cannot identify its chemical contents, and a fabric photograph does not establish safe care. The vocabulary helps him ask clearer questions before acting.
